title: Given M sorted lists of numbers, find the Kth smallest number among all of them. Explain the K-way Merge technique, the heap contents, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists (Find the Kth Smallest Across Sorted Lists)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists applies the K-way Merge pattern to produce only the first K numbers of the virtual merge rather than the full merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each list along with which list it came from and its index, then pop K times, each time pushing the next element from the same list. The Kth popped value is the answer. Time is K log M and space is M.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has M branch lists of fee amounts, each sorted. Priya wants the Kth cheapest fee overall. A clerk keeps the current cheapest unseen fee from each branch on a desk of size M, pops the cheapest, and replaces it with the next fee from that same branch. After K pops, the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pop the global minimum K times from a size-M min-heap; the Kth pop is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists applies the K-way Merge pattern to produce only the first K numbers of the virtual merge rather than the full merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each list along with which list it came from and its index, then pop K times, each time pushing the next element from the same list. The Kth popped value is the answer. Time is K log M and space is M.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has M branch lists of fee amounts, each sorted. Priya wants the Kth cheapest fee overall. A clerk keeps the current cheapest unseen fee from each branch on a desk of size M, pops the cheapest, and replaces it with the next fee from that same branch. After K pops, the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.

**One line to remember:** Pop the global minimum K times from a size-M min-heap; the Kth pop is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
We do not merge everything. We only advance the merge K steps, because the Kth smallest is revealed exactly when we have removed K elements in sorted order. The heap entry must remember three things: the value, the index of the list it came from, and the position within that list, so we can fetch the successor.

In Java we can model the entry as an int array `{value, listIndex, elementIndex}` and order the heap by the first slot: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]))`. We seed it with `pq.add(new int[]{lists.get(i).get(0), i, 0})` for each list. Then we pop K times; on each pop we read the entry, and if the element index plus one is still within that list, we push `new int[]{lists.get(li).get(ei + 1), li, ei + 1}`.

Senior nuance: guard K against the total count so we never pop more than exists, and note that the heap size is bounded by M, not by K or N, because each list contributes at most one live candidate. This is the same engine as Merge K Sorted Lists, simply stopped early at the Kth removal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fee-benchmarking study across M partner branches. Each branch already stores its processing fees sorted ascending. The analytics team needs the Kth smallest fee across all branches to set a percentile threshold, and merging every fee fully would waste work when K is small. This is exactly how Kth Smallest in M Sorted Lists works: it advances the merge only K steps.

The code defines a `FeeBenchmarkService` exposing `kthSmallest(lists, k)` returning the Kth smallest fee. A `Demo` builds three sorted fee lists and logs the fourth smallest fee.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three sorted lists: branch one 20, 60, 90; branch two 50, 70, 80; branch three 10, 40. We want the fourth smallest fee.

Step 1 — We seed the heap with the three first elements 20, 50, and 10, each tagged with its list index and position zero. The data lives in the heap, size three.

Step 2 — Pop one: the minimum is 10 from branch three. We push branch three's next, 40. Count is one. Heap holds 20, 50, 40.

Step 3 — Pop two: the minimum is 20 from branch one. We push branch one's next, 60. Count is two. Heap holds 60, 50, 40.

Step 4 — Pop three: the minimum is 40 from branch three. Branch three is exhausted, so nothing is pushed. Count is three. Heap holds 60, 50.

Step 5 — Pop four: the minimum is 50 from branch two. Count reaches four, so we stop. The fourth smallest fee is 50, shown below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:42:03 PM com.bank.benchmark.service.FeeBenchmarkService kthSmallest
INFO: Kth smallest (k=4) = 50
Oct 27, 2026 8:42:03 PM com.bank.benchmark.FeeBenchmarkApplication main
INFO: The 4th smallest fee is Rs.50
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: 3 sorted fee lists, k = 4
    B1: 20 60 90   B2: 50 70 80   B3: 10 40
    │
    ▼
  Seed min-heap with first of each list
    heap = {20, 50, 10}
    │
    ▼
  Pop k times, push successor each time
    │ pop 10 → push 40   count 1
    │ pop 20 → push 60   count 2
    │ pop 40 (B3 ends)   count 3
    │ pop 50 → STOP      count 4 ← answer
    ▼
  Output: 4th smallest fee = 50
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists is the K-way Merge pattern stopped early. Because the lists are individually sorted, the Kth smallest value is revealed exactly when I have removed K elements in global sorted order. I seed a min-heap with the first element of every list, each entry remembering which list it came from and its position, then I pop K times and after every pop I push the successor from the same list. The value of the Kth pop is the answer.

The reason this is efficient is that I never materialise the full merge. The heap holds at most M candidates, one live element per list, so each pop is log M and K pops cost K log M with M space. I explain to an interviewer that the entry has to carry the list index and element index so I can fetch the next element cheaply, and that I guard K against the total element count so I never over-pop an exhausted set of lists.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a fee-benchmarking study where each partner branch stored its fees already sorted and the analytics team needed a percentile threshold such as the Kth smallest fee. Rather than merging millions of fees, I advanced a size-M heap only K steps. Explaining that this is the same engine as merging K lists, simply halted at the Kth removal, and that the heap is bounded by the number of lists rather than by K or N, is what shows an interviewer I truly understand the K-way Merge pattern.
